nodes.name: Recite the number words in order through the teens
nodes.statement: Say the number words as separate words in their conventional order, starting at one and continuing through nineteen, with none skipped or repeated. These words must be memorized; they do not follow the decade rule that generates the later number words.
nodes.assess: With no objects present: 'Count out loud as far as you can, starting at one.' Credit an unbroken correct sequence from one through nineteen.

nodes.name: Count backward by ones
nodes.statement: Say the number words in reverse order by ones, from a given starting number down to one, with none skipped or repeated.
nodes.assess: 'Start at eight and count backward all the way to one.' Credit 'eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one' with no word skipped.

proposed_edges.rationale: Counting backward reverses the memorized forward order of number words, so the learner must already hold that order to run it in reverse.

nodes.name: Say one number word for each object in a count
nodes.statement: While counting a collection, pair each object with exactly one number word, so that every object is tagged once and no object is skipped or tagged twice.
nodes.assess: 'Count these buttons, touching each one as you count' (9 buttons scattered on the table). Credit if every button receives exactly one word and none is skipped or counted twice, whether or not the words are in the conventional order.
procedure: Point to or move one object that has not been counted, and say one number word with it.
Set that object apart, or keep track of it, as counted.
Repeat until no uncounted objects remain.

nodes.name: Exact meanings of the small number words
nodes.statement: Each of the number words one, two, and three names an exact quantity, so a learner asked for that many gives exactly that many objects.
nodes.assess: From a bowl of 10 toy fish: 'Give the bear three fish.' Credit exactly three fish (give-a-number task).

nodes.name: The last number word in a count tells how many
nodes.statement: When a collection has been counted correctly, the last number word said names how many objects are in the whole collection, not only the last object counted.
nodes.assess: After the child finishes counting 7 blocks, cover the blocks with a cloth and ask, 'How many blocks are under the cloth?' Credit 'seven' given without an attempt to recount.

proposed_edges.rationale: Saying the last word names how many only if a number word already names an exact quantity, as the words one, two and three do.
The statement applies only when every object received exactly one word, since a skipped or double-tagged object makes the last word the wrong total.
A collection counted correctly requires the number words said in their conventional order, and the last of those words is what names the total.

nodes.name: A count does not depend on order or arrangement
nodes.statement: The number of objects in a collection is the same whatever order the objects are counted in and however they are rearranged, provided none are added or removed.
nodes.assess: The child counts 7 bears in a row and says 'seven'. While the child watches, push the bears into a scattered pile, point to one in the middle, and ask, 'If you count them starting with this one, how many will you get?' Credit 'seven' without recounting.

proposed_edges.rationale: The claim that the count stays the same under any order or arrangement is about the total named by the last word, so that idea must already be in place.
The number claimed to stay the same under reordering is the number found by counting the collection, and the test starts from a completed count.

nodes.name: Each next number word is one more
nodes.statement: Each number word in the count sequence names a quantity exactly one greater than the word before it, so adding one object to a collection of n objects makes its number the word after n.
nodes.assess: Count 8 marbles together with the child, then drop them into an opaque cup. Drop in one more while the child watches. 'How many marbles are in the cup now?' Credit 'nine' without emptying the cup to recount.

proposed_edges.rationale: Adding one object makes the number the next word only if each word in the sequence names how many objects have been counted.
The statement refers to the word after n in the count sequence, so the learner must know which word follows each given word.

nodes.name: Count a collection to find how many
nodes.statement: Find how many objects are in a collection, whether arranged in a line, an array, a circle, or scattered, by counting each object once with the number words in order and answering with the last word said.
nodes.assess: 'How many shells are on this tray?' (12 shells scattered). Credit 12.
procedure: Say the number words in order, starting at one.
Pair each word with exactly one object not yet counted, keeping counted and uncounted objects apart.
Stop when every object has been counted.
Answer 'how many' with the last number word said.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step four answers how many with the last number word said, which relies on knowing the last word names the whole collection.
Step two pairs each word with exactly one uncounted object while keeping counted and uncounted objects apart, which is the tagging skill.
Step one has the learner say the number words in order starting at one, and the tray of twelve shells needs the words through twelve.

nodes.name: Count out a set of a given number
nodes.statement: Given a number word, make a set of exactly that many objects from a larger supply by counting objects out one at a time and stopping when the word just said is the given number.
nodes.assess: 'From this pile of 20 counters, put exactly 8 on the plate.' Credit exactly 8 counters on the plate.
procedure: Keep the given number word in mind.
Move objects from the supply one at a time, saying the number words in order from one.
Stop when the word just said is the given number word.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step three stops when the word just said equals the given number, which works only because the last word said names how many have been moved.
Each object moved from the supply must receive exactly one word, so no object is moved without a word or tagged twice.
Step two says the number words in order from one as objects are moved, up to the requested number such as eight.

nodes.name: Count sounds or actions
nodes.statement: Count a sequence of sounds or actions that are never present all at once, such as claps or jumps, by saying one number word with each as it happens, and tell how many there were.
nodes.assess: 'Listen and count my claps.' Clap 6 times out of the child's sight. 'How many claps?' Credit 6.

proposed_edges.rationale: Telling how many claps there were means reporting the last word said as the total, even though the claps are no longer present.
The statement requires saying one number word with each event as it happens, which is one-word-per-item tagging applied to actions instead of objects.
Each clap or jump is paired with the next number word in order, so the learner must produce the sequence while the events occur.

nodes.name: Read a written numeral
nodes.statement: Say the number word that a written single-digit numeral stands for.
nodes.assess: Point to numeral cards shown one at a time in mixed order (6, 2, 9, 0, 4). 'What number is this?' Credit the correct number word for each.

proposed_edges.rationale: Reading a numeral means saying the number word it stands for, so the learner must already know the spoken number words from one to nine.

nodes.name: Match a numeral to a set of objects
nodes.statement: A written numeral stands for how many objects are in a set, so a numeral can be paired with the set it describes and a set can be labeled with its numeral.
nodes.assess: Show the card '4' and three plates holding 3, 4, and 5 apples (arranged so the plate of 4 is not the longest row). 'Which plate has this many apples?' Credit the plate of 4.

proposed_edges.rationale: A numeral stands for how many objects are in a set, so pairing it with a set requires finding how many by counting the set.
The learner must turn the card 4 into the number word four before deciding which set that word describes.

nodes.name: Write a numeral for a spoken number
nodes.statement: Write the conventional numeral for a number word that is spoken, with digits correctly formed and not reversed.
nodes.assess: 'Write the number seven.' Then 'Write the number three.' Credit a recognizable, unreversed 7 and 3.

proposed_edges.rationale: Writing the numeral for a spoken number uses the learned link between each digit symbol and its number word, the same link used in reading.

nodes.name: Record how many with marks or drawings
nodes.statement: Record the number of objects in a set by making one mark, tally, or drawing for each object, so the record can later be used to tell how many there were.
nodes.assess: 'Make marks on this paper to remember how many cars are in the box' (5 cars). Remove the box. 'Use your paper to tell me how many cars there were.' Credit 5 marks and the answer 5.

proposed_edges.rationale: Using the record to tell how many later means counting the marks and answering with the last number word said.
Making exactly one mark for each car keeps every object paired once and none skipped or doubled, the same tagging discipline as one word per object.

nodes.name: Name a small set at a glance
nodes.statement: Name how many objects are in a set of one to about four or five that is shown too briefly to count, recognizing the number directly without seeing parts.
nodes.assess: Flash a card with 3 dots in a random arrangement for about one second, then hide it. 'How many dots?' Repeat with 1, 4, and 2. Credit the correct number word each time.

proposed_edges.rationale: Naming a briefly shown set means applying a number word that already names an exact quantity, extended here from one to three up through four or five.

nodes.name: Make a matching set after a brief glimpse, without words
nodes.statement: After seeing a set of one to about four objects briefly, make a set with the same number of objects without naming the number.
nodes.assess: Show 3 blocks for about two seconds, then cover them. Hand the child a pile of blocks: 'Make yours just like mine.' Credit exactly 3 blocks, whether or not the child says any number word.

nodes.name: Name a briefly shown set by seeing its parts
nodes.statement: Name how many objects are in a briefly shown arrangement too large to recognize at once by seeing it as small parts, each recognized at a glance, and knowing the whole they make.
nodes.assess: Flash a ten-frame card with 5 dots in the top row and 2 in the bottom for about two seconds, then hide it. 'How many dots? How did you see them?' Credit 7 with a description of parts such as 'five and two'.

proposed_edges.rationale: Knowing the whole the recognized parts make means finding the total of two sets joined together, the meaning of joining and counting all.
Knowing the whole the parts make uses known part-whole pairs, such as seeing five as parts of two and three.
Each part of the arrangement, such as the five and the two, must itself be named at a glance, which is the perceptual skill.

nodes.name: Tell which of two very unequal sets has more
nodes.statement: When one collection has at least about twice as many objects as another, tell which has more by looking, without counting.
nodes.assess: Show a plate of 3 cookies and a plate of 10 cookies of the same size, side by side, for a few seconds. 'Which plate has more cookies?' Credit the plate of 10.

nodes.name: Recognize two small sets as the same number
nodes.statement: Recognize that two collections of one to four objects have the same number, or that one has more, by looking, even when the two collections are made of different kinds of objects.
nodes.assess: Show 3 toy cars and 3 buttons, arranged differently. 'Do these have the same number, or does one have more?' Then show 3 cars and 4 buttons. Credit 'same' for the first pair and 'the buttons' for the second.

proposed_edges.rationale: Judging that three cars and three buttons are the same number requires apprehending each small set's exact quantity directly without words, even when the objects differ.

nodes.name: Compare two sets by one-to-one matching
nodes.statement: Decide whether two collections have the same number, or which has more, by pairing each object in one with an object in the other; the collection with objects left unpaired has more.
nodes.assess: Show 5 cups in a tight row and 6 saucers spread out in a longer row. 'Are there enough saucers for every cup, or are there more cups or more saucers? Show me how you know.' Credit 'more saucers' supported by pairing each cup with a saucer.
procedure: Pair one object from the first collection with one object from the second.
Repeat until one collection, or both, has no unpaired objects.
If both run out together, they have the same number; otherwise the collection with unpaired objects has more.

nodes.name: Compare two sets by counting
nodes.statement: Decide which of two collections has more objects, or whether they have the same number, by counting each collection and comparing the two counts; the one whose count comes later in the number sequence has more, whatever the size or spread of the objects.
nodes.assess: Show 6 small buttons and 4 large blocks, the blocks spread so their row is longer. 'Are there more buttons or more blocks? Count to find out.' Credit 'more buttons' supported by counts of 6 and 4.
procedure: Count the first collection and remember its number.
Count the second collection and remember its number.
If the numbers are the same, the collections are equal; otherwise the collection whose number comes later in the count sequence has more.

proposed_edges.rationale: The comparison holds whatever the size or spread of the objects, because rearranging or spreading a collection does not change its count.
Steps one and two count each collection to get its number, and the test problem counts six buttons and four blocks.
Step three decides which number comes later in the count sequence, which requires knowing the order of the number words.
The collection with the later count has more only because each next number word names exactly one more than the word before it.

nodes.name: Name a position in a line with ordinal words
nodes.statement: In a line of objects with a stated starting end, the ordinal words first, second, third, and so on through tenth name each object's position counting from that end.
nodes.assess: Line up 8 toy animals facing a toy barn. 'Which animal is fifth in line to go into the barn?' Then 'What place in line is the pig?' Credit the correct animal and the correct ordinal word.

proposed_edges.rationale: Naming an object's place means counting from the stated end and pairing exactly one word with each animal passed, such as the pig.
The ordinal words first through tenth follow the count sequence, and finding the fifth animal means counting up to five in order.

nodes.name: Length as an attribute of an object
nodes.statement: Length is the attribute of an object that tells how long, tall, or far it is from end to end, separate from its other attributes such as weight or color.
nodes.assess: Show a long thin ribbon and a short heavy block. 'Which one is longer? Which one is heavier?' Credit the ribbon as longer and the block as heavier, showing the two attributes are kept separate.

proposed_edges.rationale: Length must be seen as one attribute of an object that can be considered apart from other attributes such as weight or color.

nodes.name: Compare two lengths directly
nodes.statement: Decide which of two objects is longer or taller, or that they are the same length, by placing them side by side with one pair of ends aligned and seeing which extends farther.
nodes.assess: Give the child two pencils that differ in length by about one centimeter, laid crosswise with their ends not aligned. 'Which pencil is longer? Show me how you know.' Credit the correct pencil with the ends aligned to check.
procedure: Place the two objects side by side, both straight.
Line up one end of each at the same starting point.
Look at the other ends: the object that extends farther is longer; if the ends meet, the lengths are equal.

proposed_edges.rationale: The procedure decides which object is longer, so the learner must treat length as the attribute being compared between the two pencils.

nodes.name: Compare two weights directly
nodes.statement: Decide which of two objects is heavier, or that they weigh the same, by holding one in each hand or placing them in the two pans of a balance; the side that goes down holds the heavier object.
nodes.assess: Give the child a small, heavy stone and a large, light sponge and a pan balance. 'Which one is heavier? Show me how you know.' Credit the stone, shown with the balance or by hefting.

proposed_edges.rationale: The learner must treat weight as a separate attribute of an object, apart from its size, to say the small stone is heavier than the large sponge.

nodes.name: Order several objects by length
nodes.statement: Put three to five objects in order from shortest to longest by comparing their lengths, so each object is longer than the one before it.
nodes.assess: Give the child 5 straws of clearly different lengths in a mixed pile. 'Put these in order from the shortest to the longest.' Credit a correct order.

proposed_edges.rationale: Placing the straws in order from shortest to longest is done by comparing pairs of lengths directly, side by side with ends aligned.

nodes.name: Add to a very small hidden set without words
nodes.statement: After a set of one to three objects is hidden and one or two more are added to it out of sight, make a set that matches the new total, without naming any number.
nodes.assess: Show 2 balls, put them in an opaque box, then drop 1 more ball in while the child watches. 'Make your pile match how many are in the box now.' Credit a pile of 3, whether or not any number word is said.

proposed_edges.rationale: Making a pile that matches the new total without naming a number uses the same wordless representation of a small exact quantity, here updated after one more is added.

nodes.name: Take away from a very small hidden set without words
nodes.statement: After a set of two or three objects is hidden and one or two are removed from it, make a set that matches the number left, without naming any number.
nodes.assess: Show 3 balls, put them in an opaque box, then take 1 out while the child watches. 'Make your pile match how many are in the box now.' Credit a pile of 2, whether or not any number word is said.

proposed_edges.rationale: Making a pile that matches the number left without naming it uses the wordless representation of a small exact quantity, updated after one is removed.

nodes.name: Join two sets and count all
nodes.statement: Find the total when a set of objects is joined to another set by putting both sets together and counting every object from one.
nodes.assess: Put 3 counters on a plate, then add 2 more. 'How many counters are on the plate now?' Credit 5 found by counting the whole plate.
procedure: Make the first set with objects.
Make the second set and push it together with the first.
Count all the objects in the combined set, starting from one.
The last number word said is the total.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step three counts every object in the combined set starting from one, and the last word said is the total in step four.
Step one makes a first set of a given size, such as three counters, which is counting out a set of a given number.

nodes.name: Take objects away and count what is left
nodes.statement: Find how many remain when some objects are removed from a set by removing them and counting the objects left.
nodes.assess: Put 5 crackers on a plate. Take 2 away and set them out of reach. 'How many crackers are left on the plate?' Credit 3 found by counting the plate.
procedure: Make the starting set with objects.
Remove the number of objects to be taken away.
Count the objects that remain; the last number word said is the answer.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step three counts the objects that remain, and the last number word said is the answer.
Steps one and two make the starting set and remove exactly the given number of objects, which requires counting out a given number.

nodes.name: Solve add-to story problems with objects
nodes.statement: A story tells of a starting amount and an amount added to it and asks for the result; the learner acts the story out with objects or fingers and finds how many there are in all.
nodes.assess: 'Mia has 2 stickers. Her friend gives her 3 more stickers. How many stickers does Mia have now?' (counters available). Credit 5.

proposed_edges.rationale: Acting the story out with objects to find how many in all is joining the starting amount and the added amount and counting everything.

nodes.name: Solve take-from story problems with objects
nodes.statement: A story tells of a starting amount and an amount taken from it and asks how many are left; the learner acts the story out with objects or fingers and finds the result.
nodes.assess: 'There are 5 ducks in the pond. 2 ducks fly away. How many ducks are still in the pond?' (counters available). Credit 3.

proposed_edges.rationale: Acting the story out with objects means removing the amount taken from the starting amount and counting what is left.

nodes.name: A whole is more than either of its parts
nodes.statement: When two nonempty sets are put together, the combined set has more objects than either set alone, and splitting a set gives parts that each have fewer objects than the whole.
nodes.assess: Show a group of 4 red blocks and a group of 3 blue blocks, then push them together. Point to the red group in a separate identical picture: 'Are there more blocks all together, or more red blocks?' Credit 'more all together' without the child needing to give either number.

proposed_edges.rationale: The whole has more than a part because the part pairs off with some of the whole, leaving the other part unpaired.
The claim that the combined set has more than either part uses the idea of one collection having more than another.

nodes.name: Know the parts of numbers within 5
nodes.statement: For any whole number up to 5, quickly name the missing part when the whole and one part are known, or the whole when both parts are known, without counting.
nodes.assess: Show 5 counters, then hide some under a cup so 2 remain visible. 'There were 5. How many are hiding under the cup?' Credit 3 given quickly without lifting the cup.

proposed_edges.rationale: The whole of two known parts is the total of the two joined sets, which the join-and-count procedure finds.
The numbers two, three and five must each name an exact quantity before a learner can know which two quantities make five.
Naming a missing part or the whole depends on seeing a number as a whole made of parts, each smaller than the whole.
The missing part when the whole and one part are known is the amount left after removing that part.

nodes.name: Share a set fairly by dealing it out
nodes.statement: Share a set of objects equally among two or more recipients by giving one object to each recipient in turn until the objects run out, so every recipient ends with the same number.
nodes.assess: 'Share these 12 crackers fairly among these 3 teddy bears so each one gets the same.' Credit 4 crackers per bear, made by dealing out.
procedure: Give one object to each recipient in turn.
Go around again, one object each, while objects remain.
Stop when the objects run out; if every recipient was given an object in the last round, the shares are equal.

proposed_edges.rationale: The check that shares are equal when every recipient received an object in the last round rests on pairing objects with recipients, so unpaired objects mean unequal.

nodes.name: Make small groups of a given size
nodes.statement: From a set of objects, make groups that each contain the same given number of objects, one group at a time, until no full group can be made.
nodes.assess: 'Put these blocks into towers of 3 blocks each' (12 blocks). Credit 4 towers, each of exactly 3.

proposed_edges.rationale: Each group of the given size, such as three blocks per tower, is made by counting out exactly that many objects from the supply.

nodes.name: Match shapes that are the same shape
nodes.statement: Pick, from several shapes, the one that is the same shape as a given shape, including when the two differ in size or orientation.
nodes.assess: Show a small triangle pointing up. From a tray holding a large triangle turned on its side, a large square, a small circle, and a rectangle: 'Find the one that is the same shape as this one.' Credit the turned large triangle.

proposed_edges.rationale: Picking the same shape from several is a judgment that two figures are alike in one respect despite other differences like size.

nodes.name: Name typical circles, squares, and triangles
nodes.statement: Say the names circle, square, and triangle for typical examples of those shapes shown in their usual orientation.
nodes.assess: Show, one at a time, a circle, a square resting on a side, and an equilateral triangle resting on a side. 'What shape is this?' Credit the correct name for each.

nodes.name: Recognize a shape whatever its size or orientation
nodes.statement: Recognize every example of a familiar shape class, such as triangles, squares, rectangles, and circles, as that shape, whatever its size, orientation, or proportions, and reject figures that only resemble it.
nodes.assess: On a sheet with 12 figures (long thin triangles, a triangle standing on a vertex, a tilted square, an oval, a triangle with a curved side, an open three-sided figure), 'Color every triangle.' Credit all and only the true triangles colored.

proposed_edges.rationale: Recognizing every example whatever its size or orientation extends picking same-shaped figures despite size and turn to a whole class of shapes.
The test asks for all triangles, so the learner must have the shape class names, learned first for typical examples.
Rejecting a triangle with a curved side or an open three-sided figure requires attending to whether the sides are straight segments forming a closed boundary.

nodes.name: Identify and count the sides of a shape
nodes.statement: A side of a polygon is one of the straight segments that form its boundary, so the sides can be pointed to one by one and counted.
nodes.assess: Show a hexagon. 'Run your finger along each side of this shape. How many sides does it have?' Credit 6 with each side traced once.

proposed_edges.rationale: The sides are pointed to one at a time and counted, so the learner counts a set of segments by tagging each once and giving the last word.

nodes.name: Identify and count the corners of a shape
nodes.statement: A corner (vertex) of a polygon is a point where two of its sides meet, so the corners can be pointed to one by one and counted.
nodes.assess: Show a pentagon. 'Touch each corner of this shape. How many corners does it have?' Credit 5 with each corner touched once.

proposed_edges.rationale: The corners are touched one at a time and counted, so the learner counts a set of points with each tagged once.
A corner is defined as a point where two sides meet, so the learner must already identify the sides of the shape.

nodes.name: Decide whether two shapes are the same by comparing whole shapes
nodes.statement: Decide whether two flat shapes are exactly the same shape and size by checking that all of their parts match, for example by laying one on top of the other, not by matching only one side or part.
nodes.assess: Give the child two paper triangles that share one side length but differ in another side. 'Are these the same shape and size? Show me how you know.' Credit 'no' supported by overlaying the whole shapes and pointing to the part that does not match.

proposed_edges.rationale: Finding which side fails to match when two triangles share one side means comparing the lengths of corresponding sides with ends aligned.
Deciding two shapes are the same extends picking a shape that is the same as a given one, here requiring exact sameness of size and every part.
Laying one shape on top of the other to check all parts match requires turning or flipping a shape so it can be overlaid.

nodes.name: Build a shape from sticks for its sides
nodes.statement: Build a model of a named shape by laying straight pieces such as sticks end to end as its sides, so that the pieces meet at the corners and the figure looks like the goal shape.
nodes.assess: Give the child 6 craft sticks. 'Make a triangle with these sticks.' Credit a closed figure of three sticks meeting end to end.

proposed_edges.rationale: The sticks must meet end to end at the corners, so the learner must know where the corners of the goal shape come.
The learner must know what a triangle, square or circle looks like to judge that the built figure looks like the named goal shape.
Each stick stands for one side of the shape, so the learner must know a shape's sides are straight segments and how many it has.

nodes.name: Fill a puzzle outline where each piece is drawn
nodes.statement: Fill a puzzle in which the outline of every piece is drawn by choosing, for each outlined region, a shape piece that fits it and placing it there, turning it as needed.
nodes.assess: Give the child a picture of a house outlined with one square, one triangle, and two rectangles, and a pile of pattern blocks. 'Fill in the picture with these shapes.' Credit every outline filled by a fitting shape.

proposed_edges.rationale: Choosing a piece that fits each outlined region is picking the piece that is the same shape as the region, whatever its orientation.
Placing the chosen piece in its region requires turning, sliding or flipping it until it fits, as the statement says.

nodes.name: Put shapes together to make a larger shape
nodes.statement: Put two or more shapes together, edge to edge without gaps or overlaps, to make a larger shape or region whose inside lines are not drawn.
nodes.assess: Give the child pattern blocks and an outline of a large hexagon with no inside lines. 'Fill this shape with blocks.' Credit the outline filled with no gaps or overlaps, for example by two trapezoids or six triangles.

proposed_edges.rationale: Combining shapes to fill an outline uses the same choosing and placing of pieces as the puzzle with every piece drawn, with the dividing lines removed.
The test fills the hexagon outline with pattern blocks, and pieces must be turned or flipped until they sit edge to edge without gaps or overlaps.

nodes.name: Take a shape apart into smaller shapes
nodes.statement: Show how a shape can be made of smaller shapes by covering it with smaller pieces or naming the smaller shapes it splits into, when the shape gives clear clues such as a drawn line or an obvious split.
nodes.assess: Show a square with one diagonal drawn. 'This square is made of two smaller shapes. What shapes are they? Show me with your blocks.' Credit 'two triangles' shown with two triangle pieces covering the square.

proposed_edges.rationale: Covering a shape with smaller pieces along a drawn line is filling an outline whose inner pieces are marked.
The assessment asks the learner to name the smaller shapes the square splits into, such as two triangles.
Naming the smaller shapes, such as two triangles in a square cut on its diagonal, requires recognizing a shape in an unusual size or turn.

nodes.name: Turn or flip a shape to make it fit
nodes.statement: Make a shape fit an outline or match another shape by turning it, sliding it, or flipping it over, choosing which motion is needed.
nodes.assess: Show an outline of a right triangle with its right angle at the lower left. Hand the child a matching triangle with its right angle at the upper right. 'Make your triangle fit exactly inside the outline.' Credit a fit made by turning the triangle.

proposed_edges.rationale: Choosing a turn, slide or flip to make a triangle fit requires seeing that the turned piece is the same shape as the outline.

nodes.name: Follow directions for moving one's own body
nodes.statement: Direction words such as up, down, forward, backward, and around describe the position or movement of one's own body, so a learner can carry out a spoken direction that uses them.
nodes.assess: 'Take two steps forward. Now put your hands up. Now take one step backward.' Credit each movement made in the stated direction.

nodes.name: Use position words for where an object is
nodes.statement: Position words such as in, on, under, above, below, in front of, behind, beside, and next to describe where one object is relative to another, and the learner can both place an object as told and say where an object is.
nodes.assess: 'Put the bear behind the box.' Then place the ball under the table and ask, 'Where is the ball?' Credit the bear placed behind the box and 'under the table'.

nodes.name: See two objects as alike or different
nodes.statement: Judge whether two objects are the same kind of thing or alike in some way, and group objects that are alike.
nodes.assess: Show a toy car, a second toy car of a different color, and a spoon. 'Which two go together? Why?' Credit the two cars, with any reason that names how they are alike.

nodes.name: Name the attribute a group of objects shares
nodes.statement: Given a group of objects chosen because they share one attribute, such as color, shape, or size, name that attribute and add another object that has it.
nodes.assess: Show a red block, a red car, and a red crayon (each a different kind of object). 'How are these all alike? Find one more thing from this basket that belongs with them.' Credit 'they are red' and a red object added.

proposed_edges.rationale: Naming the attribute a group shares starts from seeing that the objects are alike, then saying in what way.

nodes.name: Sort objects by a given attribute
nodes.statement: Separate a collection into groups by a stated attribute, placing every object in the group that matches its value of that attribute and keeping to that one attribute throughout.
nodes.assess: Give the child a mixed pile of 12 buttons in three colors and two sizes. 'Sort these buttons by color.' Credit three groups, each a single color, containing every button, with sizes mixed within groups.
procedure: Make one place for each value of the stated attribute (for example, one tray per color).
Take each object in turn and put it in the place for its value of that attribute.
Continue until every object is placed.

proposed_edges.rationale: Sorting by a stated attribute such as color requires treating color as one attribute with separate values and ignoring the other attributes like size.
